summary: POC scoping focused on defining TTFT vs TPOT SLOs and a concrete measurement plan. Customer cares about p95 p99 latency targets for first token and sustained throughput under mixed workload. Decided on hybrid measurement: synthetic ramp + replay of production prompt set, with separate warm-cache and cold-cache runs. Next steps include sharing measurement artifacts, picking prompt set, and scheduling a 48h pilot to exercise TPOT and autoscaling behavior.
topics: TTFT definition and why it matters for UX
TPOT / sustained throughput and tail latency tradeoffs
Measurement methodology: synthetic vs replay, warm vs cold cache
Batching, KV cache, quantization impact on p95/p99
Acceptance criteria and guardrails for POC
transcript:
14:00:02 Jordan Lee: ok hi everyone, thanks for joining, i'm Jordan from Redwood, i'm AE on this account, quick round-robin?
14:00:09 Evan Cole: Evan here, CTO at AstraMed, hey, thanks.
14:00:12 Priya Menon: Priya, ML lead.
14:00:14 Marcus Reed: Marcus, infra. Dana Park: Dana, product.
14:00:18 Jordan Lee: Great. Samira, want to quick run the agenda?
14:00:22 Samira Gupta: Yeah, real quick. We want to lock down: what your success criteria are (TTFT vs TPOT), the workload sizing -- qps, token length distribution, target percentiles p95 p99 -- and a measurement plan so we can run a short pilot and compare variants. Also any compliance/infra limits.
14:00:42 Evan Cole: Sounds good. Our product is latency sensitive, customers notice the first token delay. Priya, can you add context?
14:00:48 Priya Menon: Sure. Our chat flows average 32 tokens output but some long docs up to 200. Most important metrics are Time-To-First-Token and 95th percentile for user-facing flows. For batch jobs (embeddings + ranking) we care about throughput and p99 under sustained load.
14:01:05 Jordan Lee: Awesome. Quick defs so we're aligned: TTFT = time from request accepted to first token delivered. TPOT in our language = time per output token or sustained per-token throughput across the response. We also talk about end-to-end p95/p99 on completion sometimes.
14:01:20 Evan Cole: Quick Q — how do we measure TTFT vs TPOT in a way that matches our real user experience, not just synthetic load?
14:01:27 Samira Gupta: Good question. We recommend a two-part measurement: 1) replay your production prompt set against the platform to get realistic distribution; 2) synthetic ramps to exercise tail behavior, different batch sizes and concurrency. Replay captures prompt variety, synthetics force stress conditions.
14:01:47 Marcus Reed: On replay — we'll need to sanitize prompts, but we can share a sampled set of 100 prompts. Is that enough?
14:01:54 Priya Menon: 100 representative prompts across short, medium, long should be fine for initial runs. We'll mark heavy doc-generation as separate group.
14:02:02 Samira Gupta: Perfect. Also important: warm-cache vs cold-cache. With chat, KV cache for recent context dramatically reduces TTFT on follow-ups. We plan separate runs: cold-start, warm-cache simulated (with injected KV preloads).
14:02:17 Dana Park: Does quantization affect TTFT much? We tested int8 and saw slower first token on some setups.
14:02:24 Liam O'Connor: It can. Quantization reduces compute per-token but sometimes adds model load/convert overhead that affects TTFT. We'll include quantization variants in the pilot matrix.
14:02:34 Evan Cole: We need concrete targets. Internal goal is p95 TTFT < 300ms, p99 < 600ms on chat front-line flows, and for TPOT we want sustained p95 token latency under 60ms/token when batching is allowed. Are those achievable assumptions?
14:02:51 Samira Gupta: Those are aggressive but potentially achievable on dedicated GPU pools with optimized kernels and batching. For hosted tier you'll see higher TTFT for cold starts. Also note TPOT is very sensitive to batch size and sequence length; 60ms/token p95 assumes average output length ~30 tokens and batch sizes of 4+ with KV cache.
14:03:10 Priya Menon: What about tail spikes when a large document request happens, or when autoscaling lags?
14:03:15 Jordan Lee: We'll define guardrails: for POC acceptance, two bands — "nominal": 95% of traffic must meet the TTFT/TPOT targets; and "grace": 99% must be below the higher threshold (e.g., p99 TTFT < 900ms). We'll also track error/retry rates and fallback occurrences.
14:03:35 Marcus Reed: For measurement, should we look at server-side timing or synth client timers? We want both, right?
14:03:41 Samira Gupta: Yes both. Server-side gives internal kernel timings (useful for debugging), client-side captures network+proxy. We'll provide instrumentation to capture first-byte-on-wire and final-byte. We'll include token-level timing in streaming traces.
14:04:00 Evan Cole: Can Redwood's console show per-route p95/p99 and token latencies?
14:04:05 Liam O'Connor: Yes, per-route and per-model dashboards, and we can export raw traces for offline analysis. We'll also tie runs to a given model version so comparisons are apples-to-apples.
14:04:18 Priya Menon: On sample sizes: how many requests to be confident on p99?
14:04:23 Samira Gupta: For p99 you need a lot of samples; we usually do a 48h run with at least 100k requests. But with replay of representative prompts we can bootstrap with 10k+ requests and then ramp to the 100k run for p99 stability.
14:04:39 Dana Park: Ok. Can you outline the pilot matrix?
14:04:42 Jordan Lee: We'll propose a matrix: 1) baseline hosted run (cold + warm), 2) dedicated nodes with batch sizes 1/4/8 and quantization none/int8, 3) autopilot with autoscale limits to test scaling delta. Each variant will run replay + synthetic ramp.
14:05:00 Evan Cole: On TPOT measurement, how do you separate model compute from queuing delay?
14:05:04 Samira Gupta: We annotate traces with queue enter/exit, kernel execution start/end. That lets us report queue-induced latency vs compute. For queuing, we'll include request age and concurrency metrics.
14:05:18 Marcus Reed: For POC acceptance, we might allow a temporary 10% overage during bursts if the fallbacks work. Is that a typical ask?
14:05:25 Liam O'Connor: Yes, it's common to allow burst grace but require safe fallbacks. We can set an SLA-style threshold for sustained periods. For example, >5 minutes of >10% overage triggers investigation but not immediate fail.
14:05:41 Priya Menon: On tooling — what load drivers do you recommend? We use Locust but open to k6 or custom scripts.
14:05:48 Samira Gupta: Locust is fine for replay; k6 is lighter for synthetic ramp. We'll provide sample scripts for both and a simple harness that collects first-byte and token timings.
14:06:00 Evan Cole: Ok, one risk: our data residency requirements prefer a private deployment, can we run the POC in Private mode?
14:06:07 Jordan Lee: Yes, Private or Dedicated — we can run the pilot in your VPC staging environment. For Private there are additional setup windows but timeline is doable. We'll document infra access steps in the next doc.
14:06:18 Dana Park: Timeline — what is realistic?
14:06:21 Jordan Lee: If we get the prompt set and staging access this week, SE can prepare the harness in 3 business days, then run pilot the following week (48h) and deliver results within 2 business days after. So overall ~2 weeks.
14:06:33 Priya Menon: Good. Regarding acceptance criteria — let's write them explicitly:
14:06:36 Priya Menon: A) p95 TTFT <= 300ms on cold/warm? (we may need different targets). B) p99 TTFT <= 900ms. C) TPOT p95 <= 60ms/token when batch size >=4. D) Sustained throughput target — we need ability to handle 300 QPS of short chat messages with <10% error rate.
14:06:55 Samira Gupta: We'll put those into the SLO table. Note we will separate "frontline chat" and "batch embed+rank" workloads and have acceptance criteria per workload.
14:07:06 Marcus Reed: For batch embed jobs, TPOT target is different. We expect throughput in terms of embeddings/sec, and p99 for job completion rather than per-token.
14:07:14 Jordan Lee: Right. We'll craft two SLO tables in the doc we send: Chat SLOs (TTFT and TPOT percentiles) and Batch SLOs (throughput and completion p99).
14:07:26 Evan Cole: Is cost impact part of the acceptance? We care about $/1M tokens and if dedicated reduces unit cost.
14:07:31 Liam O'Connor: We'll include estimated unit cost for each variant (hosted vs dedicated vs quantized) tied to your expected qps and token mix. That will be part of the pilot report.
14:07:44 Dana Park: Ok next — what about p95 vs p99 thresholds for conversation continuations where KV cache helps?
14:07:50 Samira Gupta: We'll measure both. Expect warm-cache p95 TTFT to be significantly lower; include warm/cold columns in SLO table. We might set warm p95 <= 150ms and cold p95 <= 300ms as examples.
14:08:04 Priya Menon: Can Redwood instrumentation export per-token timing to our telemetry (Datadog)?
14:08:08 Liam O'Connor: Yes, we can push metrics to your Datadog via metrics forwarder and also give raw traces for offline analysis.
14:08:17 Evan Cole: Any limitations on sequence length, concurrency, or model variants we should know about for realistic runs?
14:08:23 Samira Gupta: Long sequences increase memory and can change kernel selection; we'll note per-model max sequence length, and recommend breaking very long jobs into streaming chunks when possible. For concurrency, dedicated pools scale predictably but autoscale brings some ramp time.
14:08:39 Marcus Reed: Ok. Let's capture acceptance logic: pass if Chat SLO nominal band met for 95% of runs and error rate < 1% over the 48h pilot. If not, list remediation steps.
14:08:52 Jordan Lee: Agreed. We'll produce a POC Acceptance PDF with the pass/fail criteria and remediation checklist.
14:08:59 Dana Park: Final Q — what about measuring variability across regions? We have EU and US users.
14:09:05 Samira Gupta: We can run parallel pilots in both regions or route replayed traffic through each region. We'll need staging endpoints in each region.
14:09:16 Evan Cole: Great. Sounds clear. Jordan, can you circulate the checklist?
14:09:20 Jordan Lee: Yes. I'll send the SLO measurement checklist and sample harness by Monday.
14:09:25 Priya Menon: Thanks everyone.
14:09:28 (meeting closes)

Notes on transcript quality: there are occasional word swaps (e.g., "KV cache" transcribed as "K V cache"), and speaker labels reflect a live recording but some timestamps may drift slightly.
